title: Rewrite using exponent and radical rules
subtitle: Equivalent expressions · 16 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **16 of the official questions in Equivalent expressions are this one** — 1 Easy, 6 Medium, 9 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The expression mixes roots, fractional or negative exponents, or powers of powers.
- It's often multivariable with 'for positive values of' the variables, and the choices are the same thing written with radicals, fractional exponents or a different base.
- Sometimes you get a Roman-numeral format asking which forms are equivalent.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Convert every root to a fractional exponent (the nth root of x^m = x^(m/n)).
- 2) Apply the rules: multiply exponents when you raise a power to a power, add them when you multiply, subtract them when you divide, and apply the root to the coefficient too.
- 3) Convert back to the form the choices use and check each Roman-numeral statement separately.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Assign a positive value to each variable (e.g. x = 2, y = 3) and evaluate the original and each choice as numbers.
The equivalent ones give identical decimals.
This works even when there are several variables.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You take the root of the variable but not the coefficient (or the reverse).
Or you add exponents when you should multiply them, or apply the root twice.
On Roman-numeral questions, you stop after confirming one statement.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You take the root of the variable but not the coefficient (or the reverse).
Or you add exponents when you should multiply them, or apply the root twice.
